back: The energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond (kJ/mol); the same energy is released when it forms.

front: How do you calculate ΔH from bond energies?
back: ΔH = total energy of bonds broken − total energy of bonds made.

front: A bond-energy calculation gives a negative ΔH. What does it mean?
back: More energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking them: the reaction is exothermic.

front: A bond-energy calculation gives a positive ΔH. What does it mean?
back: More energy is taken in breaking bonds than is released making them: the reaction is endothermic.

notes: Use the C=O value, not twice a C–O single bond.

back: Four O–H bonds (two in each molecule).

front: How do you count the bonds broken in 3O₂?
back: Three O=O bonds: multiply the bonds in one molecule by the coefficient in the equation.

front: Why can unchanged bonds be left out of a bond-energy calculation?
back: They are broken and re-formed, so their energies cancel; the answer is the same either way.

front: Why are bond-energy values of ΔH only estimates?
back: Bond energies are averages over many compounds, and all substances are treated as gases.
